explanations.answer: Visions and revelations from the Lord
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul, the apostle writing this letter, says, “…I will go on to visions and revelations from the Lord.” (2 Corinthians 12:1) He just said there's nothing to gain, and he keeps going anyway. So the next part is all about what the Lord showed him.

explanations.answer: Praise he got from the other churches
explanations.explanation: Nice guess, but Paul doesn't go there. He says, “…I will go on to visions and revelations from the Lord.” (2 Corinthians 12:1) No church reviews, no testimonials. Paul skips the fan mail and heads straight to what the Lord showed him.

explanations.answer: His years of training as a Pharisee
explanations.explanation: Paul does call himself a Pharisee in Philippians 3:5, but that's not where verse 1 goes. Here he says, “…I will go on to visions and revelations from the Lord.” (2 Corinthians 12:1) So the résumé stays in the drawer, and the visions come out.

God it is. Paul says, “Whether it was in the body or out of it I do not know, but God knows.” (2 Corinthians 12:2) I love how honest that is. Paul doesn't pretend to have the answer, and he's fine saying God has it.

Timothy is named alongside Paul at the start of this letter (2 Corinthians 1:1), so I see why he came to mind. But Paul doesn't hand this question to him. He says, “Whether it was in the body or out of it I do not know, but God knows.” (2 Corinthians 12:2)

Peter, one of Jesus' apostles (Matthew 10:2), is a big name, so I get the pick. But Paul doesn't bring him up here. He says, “…I do not know, but God knows.” (2 Corinthians 12:2) When even Paul says he doesn't know, you can relax about not knowing too.

This one is False, friend. Paul says, “The things he heard were inexpressible, things that man is not permitted to tell.” (2 Corinthians 12:4) So the man was not free to share them. He heard them, but telling them was not permitted.

False is right, baker. Paul says, “The things he heard were inexpressible, things that man is not permitted to tell.” (2 Corinthians 12:4) He heard them, but he isn't permitted to pass them on. I'd be bursting at the seams, and Paul just lets it be.

True! Paul says, “…I will not boast about myself, except in my weaknesses.” (2 Corinthians 12:5) He'll brag about the man caught up to Paradise, but when it's about himself, he points to his weaknesses. That's a backwards kind of bragging, and I love it.

This one is True, baker. Paul says, “…I will not boast about myself, except in my weaknesses.” (2 Corinthians 12:5) So about himself, weaknesses are the only thing he'll boast in. Most of us would list our best moments, and Paul hands over his weaknesses instead.

That one's False, friend. Paul says, “Even if I wanted to boast, I would not be a fool, because I would be speaking the truth.” (2 Corinthians 12:6) So he says he wouldn't be a fool. He'd just be telling the truth.

False is right. Paul says, “Even if I wanted to boast, I would not be a fool, because I would be speaking the truth.” (2 Corinthians 12:6) It's the truth, so it wouldn't make him a fool. Then he holds back anyway, and that takes real strength.

Conceited, yes. Paul says, “So to keep me from becoming conceited, I was given a thorn in my flesh, a messenger of Satan, to torment me.” (2 Corinthians 12:7) That's the word he uses. Having a front-row seat to great revelations could go to anybody's head, and I'd be the first one with a crooked hat.

Discouraged sounds like a fit for a man who got tormented, but that's not the word Paul uses. He says the thorn was given “…to keep me from becoming conceited…” (2 Corinthians 12:7) It's about not getting puffed up, not about getting down.

Careless is a good try, but Paul says something different. He says the thorn was given “…to keep me from becoming conceited…” (2 Corinthians 12:7) Conceited means being too impressed with yourself, which is a different problem than being careless.

Right on, baker. Paul says, “…I was given a thorn in my flesh, a messenger of Satan, to torment me.” (2 Corinthians 12:7) He doesn't spell out what the thorn is, so I won't guess either. We know it tormented him, and we know he was given it.

A limp in the hip belongs to Jacob, Isaac's son, who walked away limping after wrestling (Genesis 32:25, 31). Paul's words are different. He says, “…I was given a thorn in my flesh…” (2 Corinthians 12:7)

I see why a thorn in the flesh sounds like a skin problem. But Paul never says what the thorn was, so I'm not going to name it for him. He says, “…I was given a thorn in my flesh, a messenger of Satan, to torment me.” (2 Corinthians 12:7) Sometimes the Bible leaves a blank, and I leave it blank right alongside it.

explanations.answer: My grace is sufficient for you
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The Lord says to Paul, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9) Paul asked three times, and that's the answer he got. It's not what he asked for, but it's what the Lord said.

explanations.answer: Keep pleading and wait on Me
explanations.explanation: That's a nice-sounding line, but it isn't what the Lord says. He tells Paul, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9) Paul pleaded three times, and the Lord's answer was grace.

explanations.answer: This thorn will soon be gone
explanations.explanation: I know that's the answer we'd all want, friend. But the Lord doesn't say that. He says, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9) That's His reply, word for word.

Weakness, baker. The Lord says, “…My power is perfected in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9) That's strange to our ears, because we expect power to show up where things are strong. But He says it plain, and Paul takes Him at His word.
Glory sounds right, doesn't it? But the Lord says, “…My power is perfected in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9) He picks the weak spot, not the shiny spot.
Patience is a good thing to have, but it's not the word here. The Lord says, “…My power is perfected in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9) Weakness is where His power shows up.

explanations.answer: So the power of Christ may rest on him
explanations.explanation: That's it. Paul says, “Therefore I will boast all the more gladly in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest on me.” (2 Corinthians 12:9) Notice the word gladly. That comes right after the Lord says, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.”

explanations.answer: So the Corinthians will pray for him
explanations.explanation: Praying for each other is a good thing, but Paul doesn't give that as his reason. He says he'll boast “…so that the power of Christ may rest on me.” (2 Corinthians 12:9) The reason he gives is Christ's power.

explanations.answer: So the false apostles will stop bragging
explanations.explanation: Good guess, since all this boasting is going on in the letter. But that's not the reason Paul gives here. He says he'll boast “…so that the power of Christ may rest on me.” (2 Corinthians 12:9) Christ's power is the whole point.

Strong, baker! Paul writes, “For when I am weak, then I am strong.” (2 Corinthians 12:10) It sounds like a riddle. Right before it, the Lord says His power is perfected in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9), and Paul says he'll boast so that the power of Christ may rest on him.
Humble fits Paul, I'll give you that. But the word he writes is a different one: “For when I am weak, then I am strong.” (2 Corinthians 12:10) That's the twist he lands on.

Alone is a heavy word, and I know that feeling. But it's not the word Paul writes. He says, “For when I am weak, then I am strong.” (2 Corinthians 12:10) And right before that, the Lord tells him, “My grace is sufficient for you…” (2 Corinthians 12:9)
